solution: Bessie never has a choice: from s she is forced along main bridges, reaching n on her (n-s)-th move while collapsing islands s, s+1, ... behind her, so before overtaking Elsie can never stand on an island >= s (those are collapsed, or occupied by Bessie, which kills her) and is confined to islands below s. Elsie therefore wins iff she can make one alternative-bridge jump from some u < s to a v strictly past Bessie's island at that instant, and arriving at u as early as possible is always best. Let d[u] be the fewest moves from island 1 to u over all bridges; since every bridge goes from a lower to a higher index, index order is a topological order and one left-to-right pass computes d[v] = min(d[v-1]+1, min over alternative edges (u,v) of d[u]+1). After Elsie's (d[u]+1)-th move Bessie stands on s+d[u]+1, so bridge (u,v) defeats Bessie exactly for starts u+1 <= s <= v-d[u]-2; marking each such interval in a difference array and prefix-summing yields all n-1 answers. Total O(n+m) time and memory, verified against an exhaustive game search over every alternative-bridge subset for n<=7 plus random tests up to n=13, and all five samples reproduce.
annotator: claude agent, verified against an exhaustive game-tree brute force

skeptic.notes:
SOLUTION: not re-litigated, but I re-derived all five samples from the stated formula and they reproduce exactly. d[] over the given graph, then bridge (u,v) defeats starts u+1 <= s <= v-d[u]-2. Sample 4 (n=10): (1,3) gives the empty range [2,1]; (1,6) gives 2..4; (2,7) gives 3..4; (3,8) gives 4..5; union {2,3,4,5} -> 100001111. Sample 5 (n=15): (2,8) -> 3..5, (4,9) -> empty since d[4]=3, (8,15) -> 9..11 since d[8]=2; union -> 11000111000111. The empty-interval cases in samples 4 and 5 are the ones a wrong off-by-one would break, and both land correctly, so the -2 is right.

dp-on-dag: KEEP, and this is the case the parallel pass's rule was written to protect, not the case it was written to exclude. The rule is 'the DAG must be one the problem hands you, not the DP's own state graph.' Here the problem hands you n islands and n-1+m one-way bridges, every one of them low index -> high index; acyclicity is stated in the input constraints (1 <= u < v <= n) rather than derived from the DP's recursion. That is the purest possible satisfaction of the rule. The three drops were state-graph DPs; this is not one of them, and the distinction is exactly the input constraint.

On the missing topological-sort companion: I checked all 49 carriers in the live corpus and confirm the pass's count -- only 13 pair with topological-sort, and the label as it actually lives here is far looser than the rule implies (cses-2229, atcoder-dp-t, leetcode-cherry-pickup, leetcode-number-of-ways-to-paint-n-3-grid are all state-graph DPs with no problem-given DAG at all). A companion that 36 of 49 carriers lack cannot be a necessary condition, and it is a symptom of the rule rather than a test of it. The direct evidence -- 'the input constraint guarantees a DAG' -- is available here and outranks the proxy. Also worth noting the corpus's own topological-sort carriers do not require a sort to be performed (leetcode-longest-increasing-path-in-a-matrix and leetcode-number-of-increasing-paths-in-a-grid both carry it over memoised DFS), so the proposer's stated reason -- 'nothing is sorted' -- is not by itself the corpus's standard.

I still decline to add topological-sort, but on a narrower ground than the proposer gave: in those memoised-DFS carriers the topological order has to be *discovered* at runtime and the traversal is the discovery. Here the order arrives free in the index labels and no step of the solution establishes it. The label should mark problems where obtaining or using an order is work; a for-loop from 1 to n is not work, and shipping this to someone searching for Kahn's algorithm is a false positive. So dp-on-dag survives unaccompanied, deliberately.

game-theory: KEEP at 0.70, and the codeforces-2257-b precedent distinguishes cleanly rather than binding. In Gigantomachy neither giant ever chooses -- each turn's move and each forward step are forced, so the whole thing is a deterministic simulation and the 'game' collapses to counting. Here Elsie has a real branching choice at every island with an alternative bridge, and the crux of the solution is an argument about her optimal play (jump as early as possible past Bessie's current island) together with a proof that Bessie's play is forced. That is one player choosing, which is precisely what 2257-b lacked.

The 'race framing is decoration over a reachability computation' worry is real but the corpus has already ruled against it twice. codeforces-329-b (Biridian Forest) keeps game-theory at 0.85 while its adversaries 'move optimally to intercept' and the entire solution is a multi-source BFS distance comparison -- decoration over reachability, kept. codeforces-1404-b (Tree Tag) keeps it at 0.90 for a pursuit game that reduces to a tree-diameter inequality. Both are the same shape as this problem: an adversarial framing that a distance criterion resolves in closed form. This one has strictly more game content than 329-b, since establishing that Bessie is forced and that Elsie prefers the earliest arrival is a genuine optimal-play argument rather than a restatement of BFS. 0.70 is honest for the collapse, and I would not raise it. Note also that even in 2257-b game-theory survived in tags after being dropped from patterns, so the search term is not at risk either way.

shortest-path: KEEP at 0.90. d[u] is literally the unweighted single-source shortest distance from island 1 over all bridges, and the entire per-bridge interval hinges on it. Co-occurrence with dp-on-dag is well precedented (codeforces-576-d, codeforces-1851-e, cses-1724, atcoder-abc137-e, leetcode-network-recovery-pathways). Not adding bfs: the distances are computed by a single left-to-right relaxation, with no queue and no frontier.

difference-array: KEEP at 0.85. Each bridge contributes one contiguous range of losing starts and the answer is their union, read out by one prefix pass -- textbook. I considered adding prefix-sum but the corpus splits 15 BOTH / 12 ONLY on that pairing, and here the prefix pass is only the readout of the difference array with no independent prefix-sum idea, so it stays a tag and not a pattern. Also declined interval-union: difference-array already covers marking-and-merging, and that label's carriers are area/measure problems.

MISSING: nothing. I agree with dropping the judge's greedy -- 'arrive at u as early as possible' is not an exchange argument, it falls straight out of d[] being a shortest distance -- and with dropping data structures, since a difference array is not one. binary-search-answer would indeed be wrong: the losing starts are a union of intervals, not a monotone predicate, which sample 5 (11000111000111) makes plain.

notes: dp-on-dag is on the graph the problem hands you (all bridges go low index -> high index), not on the DP's own state graph; topological-sort is deliberately omitted because the topological order is just the island indices and no sorting is performed. game-theory is the framing plus the crux argument about optimal play, though only one player actually has choices, so it is the least certain label. The judge's 'greedy' and 'data structures' tags are not carried: no exchange argument and no data structure beyond a difference array are needed. binary-search-answer would be wrong here despite the per-start monotone flavour.
